What’s driving the expansion of the investable universe?

Digitalization, decarbonization and deglobalization are reshaping the global economy. Artificial intelligence has become the dominant theme within digitalization, while rising energy demand has moved the focus from energy transition to energy addition. Deglobalization has sped up and expanded into data sovereignty and industrial policy.

Enormous investment is needed to support these evolving trends. That includes maintaining and modernizing existing infrastructure, as well as building new assets, such as digital networks, energy systems and more resilient supply chains. The result is a growing investable universe, spanning both traditional and newer forms of infrastructure.

Infrastructure's broadening investable universe

Infrastructure strategies generate returns primarily from three sources: cash yield, earnings growth, and multiple expansion and development. The mix of each varies across strategies, so investors can select among them based on which return drivers best align with their objectives. Infrastructure debt and core strategies offer steady cash yield, from coupon payments in the case of debt and from contracted or regulated cash flows in the case of core strategies. For core-plus and value-add strategies, earnings growth becomes a more important source of returns. It may be driven by inflation-linked pricing, volume or GDP growth, or planned capital reinvestment. Multiple expansion and development is a larger driver of returns in value-add and opportunistic strategies. It can come from operational improvements, significant capacity expansion or the development of new projects. Other market factors can also influence the timing and size of returns, including interest rates, inflation, economic growth, M&A activity and market valuations.

What does all this mean for investors?

Many existing infrastructure allocations may not fully capture this broadening investment universe, or may lack exposure to some of the most significant structural growth trends. As the asset class evolves, the objective is not simply to increase exposure to infrastructure, but to construct an integrated portfolio that reflects an investor’s specific objectives, constraints and existing exposures through a careful selection of sectors, strategies, capital structures and investment vehicles.

We believe this is an opportune time to revisit infrastructure allocations and ensure they reflect this broader opportunity set and are calibrated to best achieve portfolio objectives.
